subcomponents.title: Uses stable identities and appropriate grouped-scene architecture

subcomponents.title: Fixed-canvas uniform viewport fitting

It takes the min of the width and height ratios, and Stage applies it as `scale()` on both axes of a fixed-size canvas, so the internal coordinates never reflow. criteria.rationale: All four copies (repository and template verify and inspect) start the preview by running Vite's own bin, `node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js`, through `process.execPath` with `detached: true`. No npm or npx wrapper sits between the script and the server, so the spawned child is the preview server itself, and it leads its own process group. **verify:** `previewCommand` (lines 128-134) returns that command and `startPreview` spawns it. `stopPreview` (lines 194-208) sends SIGTERM to the whole group, races the exit against a grace period, escalates to SIGKILL if needed, and then runs `await exited`. Every exit path reaches it. Success calls `stopPreview` at line 413. A Chromium launch failure is thrown as a VerifyFailure (lines 264-268) and, like any later error, is caught at line 418. The `finally` block at lines 423-426 always calls `await stopPreview(state.handle)`. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, `cleanupOnSignal` awaits the same cleanup. **inspect:** `startPreview` (lines 384-399) spawns `process.execPath vite.js preview`, detached. `main` (lines 501-538) wraps the build, the preview, `waitForPreview` and `captureSteps` in try/catch/finally, and line 536 runs `await stopPreview(preview)`. So success, a `chromium.launch()` failure (line 450, which propagates out of `captureSteps`) and any later error all terminate the group. `stopPreview` (lines 428-443) signals the whole group and awaits the child's exit event, with a SIGKILL fallback. **Template copies:** The template copies have identical code at the same lines. `tests/unit/bootstrap-parity.test.ts` lines 67-71 assert that both scripts are byte-equal to their repository copies. **Judge C's fail is not adopted.** C relies on inspect's SIGKILL fallback not being awaited. That is a branch inside the cleanup routine, not one of the exit paths the guidance names (success, failing check, browser launch failure, later error). On every one of those paths the server process itself is signalled and its exit awaited. The un-awaited branch is reached only after SIGTERM has gone unanswered for 5 s, and SIGKILL cannot be caught. C's own evidence agrees that cleanup runs from `finally` on every path. The failure the requirement names is killing only a wrapper while the server keeps running, and that does not happen here. Judges A and B are borne out.

criteria.rationale: Judges A and B are borne out. All three clauses are met. 1. Every readiness wait is bounded. verify's waitForPreview loops only `while (Date.now() < deadline)` with READY_TIMEOUT_MS=30000 and throws on expiry, and each probe uses `http.get` with `timeout: 1000`. inspect's waitForPreview loops against a PREVIEW_READY_MS=30_000 deadline and throws InspectError on expiry. 2. The build finishes before the preview starts. verify runs the build with spawnSync, which is synchronous, in the build phase before startPreview. inspect runs `await runBuild()`, which resolves only on exit code 0, before freePort and startPreview. 3. Ready-URL parsing tolerates ANSI codes and split chunks. Both scripts append every stdout and stderr chunk to one accumulated string, strip ANSI SGR sequences from the whole string, and only then test `.includes('127.0.0.1:<port>')`. Judge C's reason is that inspect's single fetch and arrayBuffer calls have no abort timeout. Those calls are made only after Vite has printed that it is listening on the script's own port, and they sit inside a deadline-bounded loop. A server that accepts the connection but never answers is a hypothetical the candidate's Vite preview does not produce, and the guidance does not name it. The readiness wait itself has a timeout, so C's reason does not decide the requirement.

criteria.rationale: `index.ts` exports 10 public components: Presentation, Stage, Appear, Arrow, Box, Emphasis, Frame, Label, SceneLayer and SymbolChip. Each one meets all three clauses. **(1) Typed props.** Every component declares an explicit props interface: PresentationProps, StageProps, AppearProps, ArrowProps, BoxProps, EmphasisProps, FrameProps, LabelProps, SceneLayerProps and SymbolChipProps. Each has typed className (`string`), style (`CSSProperties`), children (`ReactNode`) and component-specific fields. Each extends `DataHooks`, typed as `{ [key: `data-${string}`]: string | undefined }`. None is an untyped bag such as Record<string, unknown>. **(2) Identity hooks after caller props.** In each component the caller's leftover props are spread first, as `{...dataHooks(hooks|geometry)}`. The kit's `layoutId={id}`, `data-presentation-node`, `data-presentation-id` and the other data-presentation-* hooks come after that spread, so a caller cannot override them. This covers `data-presentation-stage`/`-mode` in Stage, and `data-presentation-root`, `data-step-count`, `data-step-index` and `data-step-id` in Presentation. **(3) Kit-only props stay off the DOM.** Kit-only props are destructured out of the props object: `id`, `enter`, `Icon`, `label`, `emphasis`, `symbol`, `from`, `to`, `twoWay` and `dashed`, plus `step`, `previous`, `index`, `scale`, `mode` and `canvas` in Stage, and `steps`, `title`, `initialMode`, `attribution` and `brand` in Presentation. They are used only to compute output. The rest is passed through `dataHooks()`, which keeps only keys starting with `data-` (geometry.ts:15-17). So x/y/w/h and anything else never reach the DOM. **Judge C's fail is not adopted.** C argues the interfaces are hand-written rather than the rendered element's prop type. The guidance names the failure as typing props as "an untyped bag such as Record<string, unknown> instead of the rendered element's props". These interfaces type every prop the primitives accept and render, including className, style, children and `data-*` attributes, so they are not an untyped bag. C itself concedes the hook-ordering and kit-only-prop clauses are met. Judges A and B are borne out.

Its Assumptions section then says 'No new ambiguity was found. The ledger records no pending user decisions.' judging basis: consensus-fail

The shared Scene (TalkScene) builds on SceneLayer and the kit nodes Box, Arrow, Label, SymbolChip and Frame. votes.rationale: Grouping: steps/index.ts has a single step() factory that every one of the nine steps goes through. It sets groupKey to the constant GROUP and Scene to TalkScene. Stage calls sceneKey(step), which returns `group:${groupKey}:${sceneId(Scene)}`. All nine steps therefore get the same motion.div key, and the scene instance stays mounted and receives new props. Identity: the presentation-owned ids in entities.ts (RECTS and SEGMENTS keys, with presentAt giving each step's id list) are passed by TalkScene's renderEntity as `id` to every kit node. Box, Arrow, Label, SymbolChip and Frame forward `id` as `layoutId` and as data-presentation-id, together with `layout`. An entity present in consecutive steps keeps the same layoutId and a persistent keyed node, so it morphs in place. groupKey preserves the mount and the ENTITY ids preserve entity identity, so I did not conflate them. Every RECTS and SEGMENTS member is consumed by a rendered element. Cards 1–4 go through the default branch, and the arrows go through the SEGMENTS branch.

Stage.tsx: `<motion.div key={sceneKey(step)}>` wraps `<Scene {...props} />`.

Box.tsx, Arrow.tsx, Label.tsx, SymbolChip.tsx and Frame.tsx each set `layout` and `layoutId={id}` and `data-presentation-id={id}`.

votes.rationale: Grouping: every one of the nine steps comes from the single step() factory in steps/index.ts, which sets groupKey: GROUP and Scene: TalkScene. Navigation therefore updates that instance with the new payload instead of remounting. A single shared groupKey is correct for this one evolving scene. checks.rationale: The dissent is right that no titles or captions are checked before rendering. The `sample` phase in `runVerify` only checks the registry: it runs `checkRegistrySource` and confirms the loader file exists. The outline itself is first compared in the render phase, by `compareStep`. That fact does not decide the criterion, though. The guidance credits "a verifier that fails a missing sample with a non-zero exit at a check that reports the sample as missing or not matching the outline." It fails only a failure that "only surfaces later as an unrelated browser or render timeout." The verifier meets that bar: - **Unregistered sample:** `checkRegistrySource` throws `VerifyFailure('sample', ...)`. Output is `verify: FAIL phase=sample step=- ...`, with exit code 1. - **Outline content absent or out of order:** `checkStepCount` reports a step count that differs from the configured nine. `compareStep` reports `title is X, expected Y`, `caption is ...`, or a caption that was not rendered. Each throws `VerifyFailure('render', i, ...)`, so the output names the phase and the step, with exit code 1. These are explicit outline-mismatch checks, not unrelated timeouts. The e2e tests confirm this. 'an unregistered sample fails the sample phase' asserts a non-zero exit, `phase=sample step=-`, and the slug in the output. 'a changed normative caption...' asserts `phase=render step=8` with 'caption is'. 'out-of-order normative steps...' asserts `phase=render step=1`. The guidance does not require the comparison to happen before rendering, so the clause the dissent calls unmet is met.

Each extends `DataHooks`, typed as `{ [key: `data-${string}`]: string | undefined }`. None is an untyped bag such as Record<string, unknown>. **(2) Identity hooks after caller props.** In each component the caller's leftover props are spread first, as `{...dataHooks(hooks|geometry)}`. The kit's `layoutId={id}`, `data-presentation-node`, `data-presentation-id` and the other data-presentation-* hooks come after that spread, so a caller cannot override them. This covers `data-presentation-stage`/`-mode` in Stage, and `data-presentation-root`, `data-step-count`, `data-step-index` and `data-step-id` in Presentation. **(3) Kit-only props stay off the DOM.** Kit-only props are destructured out of the props object: `id`, `enter`, `Icon`, `label`, `emphasis`, `symbol`, `from`, `to`, `twoWay` and `dashed`, plus `step`, `previous`, `index`, `scale`, `mode` and `canvas` in Stage, and `steps`, `title`, `initialMode`, `attribution` and `brand` in Presentation. So x/y/w/h and anything else never reach the DOM. **Judge C's fail is not adopted.** C argues the interfaces are hand-written rather than the rendered element's prop type. The guidance names the failure as typing props as "an untyped bag such as Record<string, unknown> instead of the rendered element's props". These interfaces type every prop the primitives accept and render, including className, style, children and `data-*` attributes, so they are not an untyped bag. engineering-quality.rationale: `index.ts` exports 10 public components: Presentation, Stage, Appear, Arrow, Box, Emphasis, Frame, Label, SceneLayer and SymbolChip. Each one meets all three clauses. **(1) Typed props.** Every component declares an explicit props interface: PresentationProps, StageProps, AppearProps, ArrowProps, BoxProps, EmphasisProps, FrameProps, LabelProps, SceneLayerProps and SymbolChipProps. Each has typed className (`string`), style (`CSSProperties`), children (`ReactNode`) and component-specific fields. Each extends `DataHooks`, typed as `{ [key: `data-${string}`]: string | undefined }`. None is an untyped bag such as Record<string, unknown>. **(2) Identity hooks after caller props.** In each component the caller's leftover props are spread first, as `{...dataHooks(hooks|geometry)}`. The kit's `layoutId={id}`, `data-presentation-node`, `data-presentation-id` and the other data-presentation-* hooks come after that spread, so a caller cannot override them. This covers `data-presentation-stage`/`-mode` in Stage, and `data-presentation-root`, `data-step-count`, `data-step-index` and `data-step-id` in Presentation. **(3) Kit-only props stay off the DOM.** Kit-only props are destructured out of the props object: `id`, `enter`, `Icon`, `label`, `emphasis`, `symbol`, `from`, `to`, `twoWay` and `dashed`, plus `step`, `previous`, `index`, `scale`, `mode` and `canvas` in Stage, and `steps`, `title`, `initialMode`, `attribution` and `brand` in Presentation. They are used only to compute output. The rest is passed through `dataHooks()`, which keeps only keys starting with `data-` (geometry.ts:15-17). So x/y/w/h and anything else never reach the DOM. **Judge C's fail is not adopted.** C argues the interfaces are hand-written rather than the rendered element's prop type. The guidance names the failure as typing props as "an untyped bag such as Record<string, unknown> instead of the rendered element's props". These interfaces type every prop the primitives accept and render, including className, style, children and `data-*` attributes, so they are not an untyped bag. C itself concedes the hook-ordering and kit-only-prop clauses are met. Judges A and B are borne out.

verification-tooling.rationale: This is mechanism (a). The verifier reserves an ephemeral port with pickFreePort (listen(0, HOST)) and starts vite preview with --strictPort. waitForPreview accepts readiness only when the child's own output contains `127.0.0.1:<port>` and the probe succeeds. A child exit before readiness throws a VerifyFailure, and the child's exit status is rechecked after the probe answers. A stale server on the port cannot satisfy readiness on its own.

audit_results.rationale: The quoted lines meet every part of the requirement and the review guidance. (1) Sample not registered: runVerify's 'sample' phase reads src/presentations/index.ts. It throws VerifyFailure('sample', ...) when the registry file is missing, when checkRegistrySource finds no slug entry or no lazy loader, or when the loader does not resolve to a file. The catch block prints the failure via formatFailure and returns 1, and main() passes that code to process.exit. The e2e test 'an unregistered sample fails the sample phase' empties the registry. It asserts a non-zero status, no PASS line, `verify: FAIL phase=sample step=- ` and the slug in the output. (2) Outline content missing or out of order: checkStepCount rejects a step count that does not match the configured nine steps. compareStep explicitly reports a title mismatch, a missing caption, or a caption mismatch against the normative step table, as a phase=render failure with the step index. The tests show this for an out-of-order table (phase=render step=1) and a changed caption (phase=render step=8, with 'caption is'). The guidance credits any non-zero exit at a check that reports the sample as missing or not matching the outline. It fails a verifier only when the failure surfaces as an unrelated browser or render timeout. These are explicit outline-mismatch checks that name the phase and step, not timeouts. A dedicated regression test is not required when the check is explicit, and tests are quoted anyway. Judge B's point that the titles and captions are not checked before rendering is accurate. It does not make the requirement unmet, because the guidance's crediting clause does not require the check to happen before rendering.

first_results.rationale: Judges A and B are borne out. The preview server process is terminated and awaited on every exit path. In both scripts the server is Vite's own bin (vite.js) run directly with process.execPath and `detached: true`, so no npm or npx wrapper sits between the script and the server, and cleanup signals the whole process group with process.kill(-pid). verify: runVerify's `finally` runs `await stopPreview(state.handle)`. That path is taken on success, on a failing check, on a Chromium launch failure (renderSample throws a VerifyFailure from chromium.launch), and on any later error. stopPreview sends SIGTERM to the group, escalates to SIGKILL after a grace period, and always ends with `await exited`. SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers run the same cleanup. inspect: chromium.launch() runs in captureSteps outside its own try, so a launch failure or any later error propagates to main's catch and then to main's `finally { await stopPreview(preview) }`. The success return passes through the same `finally`. On each of these paths stopPreview signals the group with SIGTERM and awaits the child's 'exit' event. The bootstrap template copies are byte-equal to the repository copies, which the parity test asserts. Judge C's reason is that inspect's stopPreview does not await exit after its SIGKILL fallback. That branch runs only when the server ignores SIGTERM for 5 s. It is a sub-case the guidance does not name. On it the group still receives an uncatchable SIGKILL, so the server is terminated rather than left running. On every exit path the guidance names (success, failing check, browser launch failure, error after start), the awaited stopPreview runs, so C's reason does not decide the requirement.

first_results.rationale: Judges A and B are borne out. All three clauses are met. 1. Every readiness wait is bounded. verify's waitForPreview loops only `while (Date.now() < deadline)` with READY_TIMEOUT_MS=30000 and throws on expiry, and each probe uses `http.get` with `timeout: 1000`. inspect's waitForPreview loops against a PREVIEW_READY_MS=30_000 deadline and throws InspectError on expiry. 2. The build finishes before the preview starts. verify runs the build with spawnSync, which is synchronous, in the build phase before startPreview. inspect runs `await runBuild()`, which resolves only on exit code 0, before freePort and startPreview. 3. Ready-URL parsing tolerates ANSI codes and split chunks. Both scripts append every stdout and stderr chunk to one accumulated string, strip ANSI SGR sequences from the whole string, and only then test `.includes('127.0.0.1:<port>')`. Judge C's reason is that inspect's single fetch and arrayBuffer calls have no abort timeout. Those calls are made only after Vite has printed that it is listening on the script's own port, and they sit inside a deadline-bounded loop. A server that accepts the connection but never answers is a hypothetical the candidate's Vite preview does not produce, and the guidance does not name it. The readiness wait itself has a timeout, so C's reason does not decide the requirement.

first_results.rationale: Judges A and B are borne out. All three clauses are met. 1. Bad step counts and indices are rejected. captureSteps reads data-step-count and throws InspectError when it is missing (null), non-numeric or non-integer (`!Number.isInteger(count)`), or less than 1, which covers zero. Step indices are checked through an exact attribute selector, `[data-step-index="${index}"]`. A missing or non-numeric index can never match it, so the wait times out and throws InspectError('transition'). 2. The index is confirmed before every capture. Each iteration waits for that exact selector before page.screenshot. 3. A zero-capture success is impossible. Because count is at least 1, the loop runs and captures at least once before main can return 0. Every error goes to main's catch, which returns 1. Judge C's reason is that the helper does not reject a reported index of zero. Index 0 is the first real step of the deck. The requirement's 'zero' is about the step count, which is rejected, and an index is accepted only when it equals the index inspect meant to reach. So C's reason does not show any clause unmet.

first_results.rationale: Judges A and B are borne out. All three clauses are met. 1. Props are typed, not an untyped bag. Each public primitive (Box, Arrow, Label, Frame, SymbolChip, Emphasis, SceneLayer, Appear, Presentation) declares an explicit props interface. Its pass-through attributes use React's element types (CSSProperties style, ReactNode children, string className) and a template-literal `data-${string}` index type. None uses Record<string, unknown>. 2. Identity hooks cannot be overridden. Caller attributes are spread first, through `{...dataHooks(...)}`, and layoutId, data-presentation-id, data-presentation-node and the other kit hooks are written after that spread, so the kit's values win. 3. Kit-only props stay off the DOM. Props such as id, enter, Icon, label, emphasis, symbol, from, to, twoWay, dashed, steps, title, canvas and attribution are destructured, and the remaining rest object is filtered by dataHooks() to `data-*` keys before it is spread. Judge C's reason is that the interfaces are kit-specific rather than full element prop types. The guidance makes the failure condition an untyped bag such as Record<string, unknown>, and says 'Typed primitives that apply identity hooks after caller props and strip kit-only props pass.' These primitives are typed, and the props they forward use the element's React types, so C's reason does not show the first clause unmet.

results.rationale: All four copies (repository and template verify and inspect) start the preview by running Vite's own bin, `node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js`, through `process.execPath` with `detached: true`. No npm or npx wrapper sits between the script and the server, so the spawned child is the preview server itself, and it leads its own process group. **verify:** `previewCommand` (lines 128-134) returns that command and `startPreview` spawns it. `stopPreview` (lines 194-208) sends SIGTERM to the whole group, races the exit against a grace period, escalates to SIGKILL if needed, and then runs `await exited`. Every exit path reaches it. Success calls `stopPreview` at line 413. A Chromium launch failure is thrown as a VerifyFailure (lines 264-268) and, like any later error, is caught at line 418. The `finally` block at lines 423-426 always calls `await stopPreview(state.handle)`. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, `cleanupOnSignal` awaits the same cleanup. **inspect:** `startPreview` (lines 384-399) spawns `process.execPath vite.js preview`, detached. `main` (lines 501-538) wraps the build, the preview, `waitForPreview` and `captureSteps` in try/catch/finally, and line 536 runs `await stopPreview(preview)`. So success, a `chromium.launch()` failure (line 450, which propagates out of `captureSteps`) and any later error all terminate the group. `stopPreview` (lines 428-443) signals the whole group and awaits the child's exit event, with a SIGKILL fallback. **Template copies:** The template copies have identical code at the same lines. `tests/unit/bootstrap-parity.test.ts` lines 67-71 assert that both scripts are byte-equal to their repository copies. **Judge C's fail is not adopted.** C relies on inspect's SIGKILL fallback not being awaited. That is a branch inside the cleanup routine, not one of the exit paths the guidance names (success, failing check, browser launch failure, later error). On every one of those paths the server process itself is signalled and its exit awaited. The un-awaited branch is reached only after SIGTERM has gone unanswered for 5 s, and SIGKILL cannot be caught. C's own evidence agrees that cleanup runs from `finally` on every path. The failure the requirement names is killing only a wrapper while the server keeps running, and that does not happen here. Judges A and B are borne out.

results.rationale: Judges A and B are borne out. All three clauses are met. 1. Every readiness wait is bounded. verify's waitForPreview loops only `while (Date.now() < deadline)` with READY_TIMEOUT_MS=30000 and throws on expiry, and each probe uses `http.get` with `timeout: 1000`. inspect's waitForPreview loops against a PREVIEW_READY_MS=30_000 deadline and throws InspectError on expiry. 2. The build finishes before the preview starts. verify runs the build with spawnSync, which is synchronous, in the build phase before startPreview. inspect runs `await runBuild()`, which resolves only on exit code 0, before freePort and startPreview. 3. Ready-URL parsing tolerates ANSI codes and split chunks. Both scripts append every stdout and stderr chunk to one accumulated string, strip ANSI SGR sequences from the whole string, and only then test `.includes('127.0.0.1:<port>')`. Judge C's reason is that inspect's single fetch and arrayBuffer calls have no abort timeout. Those calls are made only after Vite has printed that it is listening on the script's own port, and they sit inside a deadline-bounded loop. A server that accepts the connection but never answers is a hypothetical the candidate's Vite preview does not produce, and the guidance does not name it. The readiness wait itself has a timeout, so C's reason does not decide the requirement.

results.rationale: Judges A and B are borne out. All three clauses are met. 1. Bad step counts and indices are rejected. captureSteps reads data-step-count and throws InspectError when it is missing (null), non-numeric or non-integer (`!Number.isInteger(count)`), or less than 1, which covers zero. Step indices are checked through an exact attribute selector, `[data-step-index="${index}"]`. A missing or non-numeric index can never match it, so the wait times out and throws InspectError('transition'). 2. The index is confirmed before every capture. Each iteration waits for that exact selector before page.screenshot. 3. A zero-capture success is impossible. Because count is at least 1, the loop runs and captures at least once before main can return 0. Every error goes to main's catch, which returns 1. Judge C's reason is that the helper does not reject a reported index of zero. Index 0 is the first real step of the deck. The requirement's 'zero' is about the step count, which is rejected, and an index is accepted only when it equals the index inspect meant to reach. So C's reason does not show any clause unmet.

results.rationale: `index.ts` exports 10 public components: Presentation, Stage, Appear, Arrow, Box, Emphasis, Frame, Label, SceneLayer and SymbolChip. Each one meets all three clauses. **(1) Typed props.** Every component declares an explicit props interface: PresentationProps, StageProps, AppearProps, ArrowProps, BoxProps, EmphasisProps, FrameProps, LabelProps, SceneLayerProps and SymbolChipProps. Each has typed className (`string`), style (`CSSProperties`), children (`ReactNode`) and component-specific fields. Each extends `DataHooks`, typed as `{ [key: `data-${string}`]: string | undefined }`. None is an untyped bag such as Record<string, unknown>. **(2) Identity hooks after caller props.** In each component the caller's leftover props are spread first, as `{...dataHooks(hooks|geometry)}`. The kit's `layoutId={id}`, `data-presentation-node`, `data-presentation-id` and the other data-presentation-* hooks come after that spread, so a caller cannot override them. This covers `data-presentation-stage`/`-mode` in Stage, and `data-presentation-root`, `data-step-count`, `data-step-index` and `data-step-id` in Presentation. **(3) Kit-only props stay off the DOM.** Kit-only props are destructured out of the props object: `id`, `enter`, `Icon`, `label`, `emphasis`, `symbol`, `from`, `to`, `twoWay` and `dashed`, plus `step`, `previous`, `index`, `scale`, `mode` and `canvas` in Stage, and `steps`, `title`, `initialMode`, `attribution` and `brand` in Presentation. They are used only to compute output. The rest is passed through `dataHooks()`, which keeps only keys starting with `data-` (geometry.ts:15-17). So x/y/w/h and anything else never reach the DOM. **Judge C's fail is not adopted.** C argues the interfaces are hand-written rather than the rendered element's prop type. The guidance names the failure as typing props as "an untyped bag such as Record<string, unknown> instead of the rendered element's props". These interfaces type every prop the primitives accept and render, including className, style, children and `data-*` attributes, so they are not an untyped bag. C itself concedes the hook-ordering and kit-only-prop clauses are met. Judges A and B are borne out.
